extracted.intended_audience: Current or prospective mathematics department chairs (academic mathematicians) and senior faculty moving into chair/administrative roles
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for serving effectively as a Math Department Chair: communicating with Deans, planning hiring, running reviews, managing time and reputation, and balancing research and life while in office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate with the Dean in Dean-language
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the points that are obvious to a mathematician ... your implicit focus and instead play up programmatic needs, new majors, new job opportunities for graduate students, and new directions in science overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pitch in the technical language of arithmetic/algebraic geometry/string theory. Frame proposals in terms the Dean values (benefit to College, undergraduates, campus priorities). Have Executive Committee help translate mathematical priorities into Dean-talk. Avoid sounding like 'Gimme, gimme, gimme.' Show you are a team player and take the broad view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weave departmental benefits into college-friendly proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are clever, then good things for the Math Department will be woven into any pitch that you put to the Dean; but the overall gloss will be that this is something that is good for the College and good for the Undergraduate students (or whatever segment of the University population you may choose to benefit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present departmental requests as aligned with college-wide goals; highlight programmatic and student benefits while embedding specific math needs subtly. This increases receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term hiring plan (prefer five-year plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deans like long-term planning. Rather than go to the Dean each year with a narrow, limited view of what hiring you would like to do right now, you will find it better received to have a five-year plan for hiring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for (i) upcoming retirements, (ii) impending tenure cases, (iii) new scholarly developments, (iv) hot-breaking fields, (v) long-term medical issues, (vi) disability issues. Present hires in a strategic multi-year context instead of one-off requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that position replacements are not automatic
rubrics_metrics.description: If Professor Beans retires... that is no guarantee that the Department will get the position restored in order to replace the lost individual. The Chair must argue for each new position as though it were from scratch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never assume a vacated line is guaranteed. The one exemption is the intended replacement after an Assistant Professor is terminated for non-tenure—but even that 'sacred' trust may not always be honored in practice. Plan and argue accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare meticulously for meetings with the Dean
rubrics_metrics.description: Always prepare for meetings with the Dean. Deans have an uncanny ability to be on top of all sorts of information and statistics that you’ve never even heard of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the topic in advance, have relevant information/statistics at your fingertips, bring written copies of proposals (multiple copies), be ready to leave a memo or get immediate sign-off, and send a follow-up memo summarizing agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document significant conversations (memos as insurance)
rubrics_metrics.description: After you have a meeting... send him a memo summarizing what was said and what agreements might have been reached. The memo is just insurance that everyone remembers the meeting in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use memos after significant meetings with the Dean and with colleagues about raises, teaching assignments, or other substantive issues. For routine social chats memos aren't needed. Keep written records to protect yourself and clarify expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence and manage external/departmental reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Good universities have regular outside reviews.... The Chair can have an effect: recommend committee members, schedule activities, assemble proper materials, form a Taskforce to prepare, and meet with the Dean to plan the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the review committee has the information it needs (faculty research, recent Ph.D.s, majors, grants, invitations, editorial/national service). Use discretion in shaping the review (who they talk to and how they spend their time) and aim to have the report come out favorably, since it influences future hiring and administration decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow Departmental Bylaws and Mission Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Departments will have a formal document that comprises the Departmental Bylaws... The Department may also have a Mission Statement... It talks about the role of the faculty and the role of the Chair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know whether the Department expects you to run according to those rules. Do not ignore bylaws lightly; understand the mission versus bylaws distinction (mission is philosophical; bylaws are procedural) and operate within them when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegate and manage your time; avoid constant task-switching
rubrics_metrics.description: You must learn serious time management skills... The wrong way is to jump from Task A to B to C reminding yourself of each but accomplishing nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan each workday with specific tasks and time blocks (e.g., allocate 2, 3, and 2 hours for selected tasks). Set aside uninterrupted chunks for focused work. Delegate work to colleagues and staff where appropriate and ensure tasks are completed rather than personally doing everything.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide promptly on service assignments (e.g., refereeing)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are asked to referee a paper, decide right away: either decline immediately (so you get it off your desk) or accept and set aside the required couple of hours to do the job properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repeatedly re-examining a request without acting. Immediate decisions free up cognitive load and prevent wasted small time-slices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect focused research time; large chunks needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a successful publishing program requires good time management—you can’t prove theorems and write papers by snatching a 20-minute time interval here and there. You really need large chunks of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want to continue an active research program while Chair, reserve regular blocks (e.g., one or two afternoons a week) for research. Attend seminars and maintain collaborations to stay engaged; consider changing fields periodically to stay fresh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain work–life balance and set aside personal time
rubrics_metrics.description: Your life has many dimensions. Becoming Chair may cause you to emphasize some and minimize others... You must learn serious time management skills in order to maintain a balance in your life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegate, set aside one or two afternoons per week for yourself (phone off the hook if necessary), keep spouse/partner and family needs in mind, continue diversions. Chairs should try to preserve personal life to avoid burnout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use support staff effectively (secretary/protections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any Chair should have a secretary who protects him/her from the great unwashed, and helps him/her to manage his/her time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let staff screen interruptions, schedule meetings, and protect closed-door work times. Establish regular 'receive company' times and closed-door work times to control availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit teaching consciously while Chair (balance expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: I have always taken it as axiomatic that a Chair teaches little or not at all... I always taught one course per year... Many Chairs do not teach at all and have no trouble justifying this policy. Your Dean may have other ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide early what teaching load you will carry as Chair. If you teach, choose low-preparation/high-impact courses (e.g., a teaching course for grad students) and use teaching choices to signal departmental values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using resignation as a bargaining cudgel
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Chairs take comfort in knowing that they can resign and plan to use this as a cudgel... I personally think this is wrong-headed. Resigning should really be the action of last resort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate commitment; threats to resign weaken standing with both Dean and colleagues and can damage the Department. Reserve resignation for genuine last-resort situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent the Department with dignity and appropriate demeanor
rubrics_metrics.description: You are the face of the Math Department... You can no longer be the Departmental hothead... You need to comport yourself at meetings—in fact all day long—with dignity and grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt professional dress and behavior (avoid cutoff tees, etc.), be prepared for impromptu meetings with important visitors, and cultivate a public persona the Department can be proud of.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate an initial term strategically (suggest five years)
rubrics_metrics.description: The smart thing to do when you agree to serve as Chair... is to say that you will serve an initial five years, after which you can both assess the situation and see how everyone feels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A three-year term can leave you with only one effective year; five years gives time to implement plans. Be aware Deans may prefer longer-serving, reliable chairs; negotiate to keep options open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage risks of second (and later) terms (avoid hubris)
rubrics_metrics.description: One bad feature of a second term... is that you can get cocky... You cannot always trust the Dean. Always first run new policies by your Executive Committee and other trusted colleagues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult Executive Committee before major unilateral changes. Avoid abrupt announcements of sweeping policies. Build infrastructure and ensure Dean backing before implementation. Remain humble and collegial to retain trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid policies announced without faculty buy-in
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chair who announced 'Teaching Faculty and Research Faculty' to the department cold provoked unified outrage; the policy succeeded later when a politically savvy Chair quietly implemented it with groundwork and Dean support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First consult colleagues and Executive Committee; pilot infrastructure and reward systems; ensure clear communication and prior buy-in before rolling out structural changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be realistic about path to higher administration (Dean/Provost)
rubrics_metrics.description: Being Chair is relatively easy to get; the Deanship has more competition and is a major life change... Those are big jobs, often requiring that you work seven days a week. Think carefully before embarking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider workload, loss of summers, political realities, and increased scrutiny. Recognize that former colleagues expect objectivity and that initial actions may be tough on your old department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against becoming stale or self-serving in long tenure as Chair
rubrics_metrics.description: After a while you will become jaded... you will do less for the Department and more to feather your own nest... For most of us, two terms is plenty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit service length to avoid loss of effectiveness; maintain fairness and avoid decisions that prioritize personal agendas. Consider stepping down after two terms to return to scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use outside committee reports strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: An outside Committee report can be a great thing; it really carries some weight with the Dean... It will have a decided effect on the Department’s future (in particular, on future hiring). Use what discretion you have as Chair to make sure it comes out right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare materials and shape reviewer interactions to produce a report that aligns with department aims, while respecting the committee's independence. Coordinate with Dean to set mutually agreeable goals for the review.
